newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: FEATURE - Fat stays put at Guatemalan weight clinics.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fat stays put at Guatemalan weight clinics.

text.p: For overweight women with money to burn but no taste for calorie-burning exercise, a growing number of luxury Guatemalan clinics say they have the answer to get-thin-fast dreams.

"Electroliposuction," reducing massage, sweat-inducing girdles, plaster casts, wraps and a technique called "Egyptian embalming," which sounds like the longest-lasting weight-loss method short of death, have replaced diets, the clinics say.
While fat substitutes, often with queasy side effects, are all the rage in the United States, Guatemalans are falling prey to surface treatments doctors say are quackery.

"These places are a threat," physician and nutritionist Marina Cornejo said of a dozen clinics that have opened in recent years. Consumer rights groups say they have not had complaints about the clinics, but Cornejo and other doctors said the treatments produce dehydration and empty pockets rather than dream figures.

The clinics cater to middle and upper-class Guatemalan women in wealthier parts of the capital. They charge $200 for a month-long package of massages and "electronic therapies" in a city where the average live-in maid earns $100 a month.

"The prices are extremely high. I've had a lot of patients who have gone to get bandages and massages and they've lost weight but they put it right back on," licensed nutritionist Karen Altalef told Reuters.

Lax advertising regulations and scarce medical information on diet and exercise make the clinics a lucrative business. Cornejo says the association of Guatemalan medical doctors refuses to speak out against the clinics.
CONSUMER OFFICE HAS NO MUSCLE

Carlos Hernandez, who runs the Economy Ministry's consumer protection department, acknowledges that the clinics should be investigated but says his office has no muscle when it comes to controlling deceptive advertising.

One clinic runs an ad promising women they will win back their husbands' lost affections. Others offer seemingly impossible guarantees. "This super-intensive treatment will make you lose two sizes in just five days. One session is enough. We guarantee a perfect figure," screams one large newspaper ad picturing a bikini blond with tight tummy and gravity-defying breasts.

Charm, a weight clinic and spa, advertises an exclusive treatment called "hypothermic Egyptian embalming. The most innovative treatment that acts against cellulite and reduces and firms-up specific areas."

Another clinic, Biomedica, runs ads showing an obese woman reclining on a couch with gigantic rolls of fat exploding out of her skimpy bodysuit. Tiny print at the bottom of the ad assures Guatemalans that this is a "North American model."

"We achieve ideal measurements," said Ligia de Ramirez, the enthusiastic proprietor of the Biomedica clinic in a high-rise tower in a high-rent district. She is careful not to guarantee weight loss but claims inches off hips and thighs. The secret of her success is a type of reducing massage invented by her husband, she says.

Martita, who said she is too lazy to exercise, is sure the 25 minutes a week of massage help her, even though she has not shed any pounds. "I haven't really lost weight because I cheated on the diet recommendations but all of my measurements have gone down a lot," the 30-year-old Biomedica client said.
'ALL I GOT WAS BRUISES'

But at least one disappointed Biomedica customer said the treatments were a waste of money. "All that happened with the massages was I got bruises all over my body," said the woman, who did not want to be identified.

Doctors and nutritionists say believing in these treatments could make you fatter, not thinner. "The biggest danger is to accelarate your metabolism and end up weighing even more than you did at first," Altalef said.

Classical Greek-inspired statues and small fountains lend a spa-like atmosphere to another clinic, Perfect Form. Beyond the airy entrance, a rabbit warren of rooms house gleaming science fiction-type machines that supposedly zap fat with light electric currents.

Owner Dina Colindra told Reuters the country's top models and beauty queens, including Miss Guatemala, come here for "electroliposuction," a non-surgical treatment in which bands of insulated wires are wrapped around the body.
"It's like exercise. You feel muscular contractions," Colindra said. She also said these electronic treatments provoke a "lymphatic drainage that eliminates toxins."
She said another treatment, thick wraps, lowers the body temperature and burns 1000 calories in half an hour.
"Scientifically there is no explanation of how this works," said Cornejo, whose office is full of a different kind of machine -- exercise bicycles.
